name: Bahia
summary_text: Bahia is a state in north-east Brazil and stands under the national framework described above: the federal constitutional and criminal prohibitions on SOGI discrimination, the 2018 removal of the surgical requirement for legal gender change, equal age of consent, same-sex marriage and spousal-visa equality, and National Council of Justice Resolution 348/366 governing the placement of LGBTI detainees all extend to Bahia and to its prison system.  Bahia records one of the country's highest burdens of trans and travesti killings. The ANTRA 2025 dossier, reported by SBT News on 26 January 2026, counts 7 trans people killed in Bahia during 2025, behind only the states recording 8; on the same national reckoning, which counts 1,261 killings across Brazil from 2017 to 2025, Bahia ranks third with 97, after São Paulo at 151 and Ceará at 107. Valor Internacional recorded the same state-level counts on 27 January 2026, placing Bahia behind the Ceará and Minas Gerais pair.  The figure is persistent rather than a single-year outlier. The ANTRA dossier for 2022 ranked Bahia seventh among the Brazilian states, with 7 killings of travestis recorded in the state that year, putting Bahia in the top band of consecutive annual dossiers.  Individual cases show how the violence is charged and processed. On the weekend of 6–7 December 2025, Rhianna, an 18-year-old trans woman, was choked to death in Luís Eduardo Magalhães, in the west of Bahia. The suspect, a 19-year-old app driver, drove the victim's body to the police station himself, confessed, and claimed self-defence; he was released. The Civil Police confirmed that the case is being investigated as a feminicide, and the state police framed the killing as gender-based, so the killing of a trans woman in Bahia was classified as gender-based violence while the accused was initially set free.  For a trans visitor, the practical exposure is the violence risk and its investigative handling rather than any entry, document or visa rule: the national framework applies Bahia's entry and family-law treatment on the same footing as for anyone else, and no Bahia-specific rule governing where trans detainees are held was located in the sources reviewed.

name: Ceara
summary_text: Ceará stands under Brazil's national framework for LGBTI people. The Constitution, the Penal Code and federal anti-discrimination provisions apply in the state, and no Ceará-specific statute distinguishes gender identity or expression. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and an expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate across the country. A trans visitor's documents and family status are therefore handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in registry matters.  After the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. Ceará is bound by those provisions like every other state, and there is no indication in the sources of a state law or state policy cutting back on them.  The violence record is the sharpest finding for a visitor. Reporting by G1/Globo on 28 January 2025, citing the ANTRA dossier, identifies Ceará as the Northeast state with the most killings of trans people in 2024: 11 killings, the third highest count in the country. The following year did not reverse the pattern. Igbá Agência reported on 26 January 2026, and SBT News the same day, that the ninth ANTRA dossier placed Ceará among the states with the most trans killings in 2025 with 8 cases, tied with Minas Gerais at the top of the state ranking.  National totals give those figures their scale. Brazil recorded 80 trans killings in 2025, an 18th consecutive year as the country with the highest number worldwide and a 34 per cent fall from 2024. Between 2017 and 2025 the count reached 1,261, an average near 140 a year. The victims are overwhelmingly racialised: of the 57 victims with race data in the 2025 dossier, 70 per cent were Black, against an average of 77 per cent across 2017 to 2025.  Detention in Ceará is governed by a specific national regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, fixes where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is set by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted: the judge must list the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, placement can be changed later, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.  Practice does not reliably follow that framework anywhere in the country. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women in Rio de Janeiro state prisons, carried out between April and June 2021, interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units operated as masculine in the metropolitan region, documenting placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. The study also records a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, and national norms from 2014 and 2020 permitting people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine. No equivalent census for Ceará's prisons is available in the sources.
